---
title: Toyota Corporate History
author: Reference notes compiled for the Toyota RAG project

# Chapter 1: From Looms to Automobiles (1867-1937)

Sakichi Toyoda was born in 1867 in a village in what is now Kosai, Shizuoka Prefecture. The son of a carpenter, he devoted his life to improving weaving looms. He patented a wooden hand loom in 1891 and Japan's first power loom in 1896. In 1926 he founded Toyoda Automatic Loom Works to manufacture his Type G automatic loom. In 1929 the rights to the loom were sold to the British company Platt Brothers, and part of the proceeds helped fund research into automobiles.

Sakichi's eldest son, Kiichiro Toyoda, was an engineer who had studied mechanical engineering at Tokyo Imperial University. Convinced that Japan needed its own car industry, Kiichiro established an automobile department within Toyoda Automatic Loom Works in 1933. The department built its first prototype passenger car, the Model A1, in 1935, and the G1 truck went on sale the same year. In 1936 the Model AA passenger car entered production.

Toyota Motor Co., Ltd. was established as an independent company in August 1937, with Kiichiro Toyoda later becoming its president. The company chose the name "Toyota" rather than the family name "Toyoda". The new name sounded clearer, separated the business from the family's private life, and in katakana it is written with eight strokes, a number considered lucky in Japan.

# Chapter 2: War, Crisis and Recovery (1937-1960)

During the Second World War Toyota was ordered to concentrate on trucks for the military. After the war the company restarted passenger-car development, but the Japanese economy was in deep trouble.

In 1949 and 1950 Toyota faced a severe financial crisis. Sales collapsed under deflationary government policies, and the company was close to bankruptcy. A bank consortium arranged rescue financing on the condition that the company cut costs, separate its sales operation into a separate company (Toyota Motor Sales) and reduce its workforce. A long labour dispute followed. In 1950 Kiichiro Toyoda resigned as president, taking responsibility for the layoffs. Shortly afterwards, demand for trucks during the Korean War brought large orders and helped the company recover. The experience of nearly going bankrupt left a lasting mark: Toyota has since been known for keeping large cash reserves and for its commitment to job security.

Also in 1950, Eiji Toyoda, Kiichiro's cousin, spent several months studying Ford's River Rouge complex in Michigan. He concluded that Toyota could not copy Ford's mass production directly, but could learn from it and improve on it. Eiji and Taiichi Ohno then pushed the development of the Toyota Production System. Eiji later served as president from 1967 and as chairman from 1982.

The Toyopet Crown, launched in 1955, was the first passenger car designed and built entirely in-house by Toyota using Japanese technology. Toyota first exported cars to the United States in 1957-1958, but the early Crown was underpowered for American highways and sales were poor.

# Chapter 3: Global Expansion (1960-1990)

The Corolla, launched in 1966, became one of the most important cars in automotive history. It was designed as an affordable, reliable family car for a Japan entering mass motorisation. The Corolla went on to become the best-selling car nameplate in the world, with cumulative sales of well over 50 million units across many generations.

During the oil crises of the 1970s, demand for small, fuel-efficient cars grew rapidly in North America and Europe, and Toyota's exports rose sharply. Trade friction with the United States led Toyota to begin manufacturing there. In 1984 Toyota and General Motors opened NUMMI (New United Motor Manufacturing, Inc.) in Fremont, California. Toyota then opened its own plant in Georgetown, Kentucky, which began production in 1988 and became Toyota's largest plant outside Japan.

In 1982 Toyota Motor Co. and Toyota Motor Sales merged to form Toyota Motor Corporation, the company's current name. Shoichiro Toyoda, Kiichiro's son, became president of the merged company.

In 1989 Toyota launched the Lexus brand in the United States with the LS 400 luxury sedan. The project, which had begun in 1983 under the code name F1 ("Flagship One"), aimed to beat the best German luxury cars on quietness, quality and refinement. Lexus quickly became one of the best-selling luxury brands in the US.

# Chapter 4: Hybrids and Becoming the Largest Automaker (1990-2008)

In the early 1990s Toyota started the G21 project to design a car for the 21st century. Under the leadership of chief engineer Takeshi Uchiyamada, the project became the Prius, the world's first mass-produced hybrid passenger car, which went on sale in Japan in December 1997. It was introduced in the United States and other markets in 2000. The second-generation Prius, launched in 2003, made the car a global symbol of environmental awareness.

Through the 2000s Toyota expanded production around the world and gained market share in North America, Europe and Asia. In 2008 Toyota overtook General Motors to become the world's largest automaker by global vehicle sales, ending GM's decades-long position at the top.

# Chapter 5: Recalls and Rebuilding (2009-2020)

Akio Toyoda, grandson of Kiichiro Toyoda, became president of Toyota Motor Corporation in June 2009. He took over during the global financial crisis, when Toyota posted its first operating loss in decades.

Between 2009 and 2011 Toyota recalled millions of vehicles worldwide over unintended acceleration, which was linked to floor mats that could trap the accelerator pedal and to sticky pedal mechanisms. In February 2010 Akio Toyoda testified before the United States Congress and apologised. Studies by US authorities, including NASA engineers working with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, did not find an electronic cause, but the crisis damaged Toyota's reputation for quality. In 2014 Toyota agreed to pay a 1.2 billion US dollar penalty to settle a US criminal investigation into how it disclosed the problems.

Toyota responded by appointing regional chief quality officers, giving regions more authority and slowing its growth. Akio Toyoda's slogan became "ever-better cars". In 2011 the Great East Japan Earthquake and tsunami disrupted Toyota's supply chain severely, and the company afterwards built a database to map its suppliers' locations down to multiple tiers.

In 2015 Toyota introduced the Toyota New Global Architecture (TNGA), a modular approach to vehicle platforms and powertrains designed to share components across models, lower the centre of gravity and improve driving dynamics. The fourth-generation Prius was the first car built on TNGA.

# Chapter 6: Toyota Today (2020-present)

Toyota regained its position as the world's top-selling automaker in 2020 and has remained at or near the top since then, selling roughly ten million vehicles a year across the Toyota, Lexus, Daihatsu and Hino brands.

In April 2023 Koji Sato, previously the president of Lexus and Gazoo Racing, became president and CEO of Toyota Motor Corporation, while Akio Toyoda became chairman of the board.

Toyota describes its environmental strategy as a "multi-pathway" approach. Rather than betting only on battery electric vehicles, it offers hybrids, plug-in hybrids, battery electric vehicles and hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles, arguing that the best choice depends on local energy supply, infrastructure and customer needs. In 2015 the company published the Toyota Environmental Challenge 2050, which set long-term goals including reducing CO2 emissions across the vehicle life cycle and from its plants.

Toyota's headquarters are in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture, Japan. The city was called Koromo until 1959, when it was renamed after the company.
